commands.desc: Asks Rancher to upgrade the Helm release <release> in --namespace on --cluster through the upgrade action of a ClusterRepo: Rancher fetches the chart version and runs Helm in a pod. A newer version, an older version (a downgrade) and a change of values are all upgrades; Rancher has no rollback action. The server has no dry-run for this action; the preview comes from server reads (previewSource serverReads): the App (it must exist, with the status deployed, failed or superseded), the ClusterRepo (it must be enabled), the chart and version in the index Rancher serves for the cluster, the chart's default values and annotations, the Helm release Secret the App's owner reference names (it holds the release's values), and the operations of the namespace (none may still be running for the release). It carries no resourceVersion precondition: --apply reads the App, the operations and the index entry again before it sends the request, and without --wait nothing checks for a change after that. The chart is the App's chart; --chart is accepted only with that name, and another chart is refused: install it as a new release with `rancher app install`. --repo defaults to the ClusterRepo named in the App's catalog.cattle.io/ui-source-repo annotation, and --version to the App's installed version. The upgrade accepts the installed version when the index Rancher serves for the cluster no longer lists it and the ClusterRepo is the one the App came from. The preview and the result then warn that its chart content is not compared between the preview and the request. An older --version than the installed version is a downgrade, which the preview names. Values: the release's values are the values the App's revision was installed or upgraded with. The command reads them from the release Secret through the Steve API with includeHelmData=true. It merges each --values file over them in order (- reads stdin once; null removes a key) and sends the result. That read needs permission to get Secrets in the release's namespace. Without it the command stops and names --reset-values. --reset-values sends only the --values files and the values rancher-cli adds, and Helm takes every other value from the chart's defaults. rancher-cli never asks Helm to reuse the release's values. After a failed upgrade the release's values are the values that failed, and the preview warns. The preview lists the path of every value that is added, removed or changed, never the values, except the values rancher-cli adds and the registry host, and counts the release's values that it sends unchanged. As the Rancher UI does, rancher-cli adds the cluster values and the registry values the release's values lack; --system-default-registry <host> sets both registry values over the release's values, and --no-system-default-registry sends neither. The Rancher UI sends only the difference from the chart's defaults; rancher-cli sends the release's values in full. Helm treats both requests the same, and the values Helm keeps with the next revision then differ from the ones the Rancher UI would keep. Refused: an App with the status uninstalled, uninstalling, pending-install, pending-upgrade, pending-rollback or unknown, an operation still running for the release, a chart that names another chart to install first (catalog.cattle.io/auto-install or auto-install-gvr), a version whose catalog.cattle.io/namespace or release-name annotation does not match the release (the installed version is exempt), a requires-gvr or permits-os annotation the target does not meet, --force with --take-ownership, and a request that changes nothing. These flags make no change: --wait, --timeout, --cluster, --namespace, --dry-run, --apply and --yes. --version and --repo make a change when they differ from the App, and --values when the merge changes a value. Every other flag makes a change. --helm-wait (default true; --helm-wait=false sends false) makes Helm wait for the chart's resources; --helm-timeout (default 10m, at least 1s, at most 15m) is Helm's timeout; the chart's hooks can make a run longer, and Rancher removes a run's access one hour after the operation starts. --history-max (1 to 100; Rancher uses 5 when it is omitted) is the maximum number of revisions Helm keeps for the release; Helm deletes the oldest before the run, never the last deployed one. Helm does not roll back a failed upgrade: the resources it already changed stay changed, and --cleanup-on-fail deletes only the resources the upgrade created. Without --wait the command returns once Rancher accepts the request, with the operation and the commands that follow it. With --wait (or --timeout, default 55m, at most 55m) it returns when Helm's run has finished: with the release's revision and status, or with Helm's error, the release's state and the command to run next.
examples: rancher app upgrade my-nginx --cluster prod --namespace web --values change.yaml --dry-run
rancher app upgrade my-nginx --cluster prod --namespace web --version 1.2.3 --apply --yes

commands.desc: Lists container images referenced by active pods (status.phase Running or Pending; Succeeded and Failed pods are excluded, terminating pods are included until they are deleted), reading spec.containers, spec.initContainers, and spec.ephemeralContainers. --match filters by case-sensitive substring over the image reference exactly as written in the pod spec. It is repeatable, and an image matches when it contains any of the values. A short reference is not expanded to a full registry name (a bare nginx:1.25 does not match docker.io). End a value with / or : to avoid matching a longer name that starts the same way: --match registry.old.corp/ does not match registry.old.corp.example/app:1. --match never inspects image contents. --by workload starts at each pod's ownerReferences entry with controller: true (the first entry when none is marked) and moves up: from a ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet or Job it continues to that object's own owner (for example pod to ReplicaSet to Deployment), and it stops at an owner of any other kind. It reports one row per image and owning workload object (apiVersion, kind, name, uid), the last owner it reaches, with the count of pods controlled by exactly that object. When an owner cannot be read, its reference has no uid, or its uid differs from the reference, the row names the pod's direct owner instead and a warning is added. If you cannot read part of the data, the command still exits 0: each section it could not read in full is named in data.degraded ({section, state, code, target}), and each entry has one warning. With --cluster, finding the cluster by id or name and listing the pods are required: the command fails when any of them fails. With --all-clusters, listing the clusters is required, a list with no clusters succeeds with no rows, and the command fails when none of the listed clusters can be read. Sections that can degrade: ownerResolution (partial, target = the owner's apiVersion|kind|namespace|name|uid, prefixed with the cluster id under --all-clusters), clusters (partial, target = cluster id, --all-clusters only).

commands.desc: One document answering what state a cluster is in, what it is made of, and how nodes join it: the management.cattle.io Cluster's id, name, state, and kubernetesVersion (the observed version first, then the provisioning spec's desired version for pending clusters, empty when neither exists), its agent connectivity (agent.connected and agent.ready from the management.cattle.io Cluster's Connected and Ready conditions with the failing condition's message, preferring Connected's; the section is present only when those conditions report an explicit True or False (a condition with status Unknown is ignored and never shows the agent as not connected) and each field only when its own condition does; an agent that is not connected or a False Ready condition adds a warning - the status of the provisioning.cattle.io Cluster cannot show an agent outage), the provisioning.cattle.io Cluster's ready flag (derived from the Ready condition when present; falls back to status.ready) and conditions, its machine pools (name, machineConfigRef, quantity, roles), its members (ClusterRoleTemplateBindings with display names resolved from Users and UserAttributes, each row reporting principal, displayName, role, binding (the name of the ClusterRoleTemplateBinding), and system; a failed binding read leaves the members field out of the JSON while the text output shows members: unavailable, with a warning naming the cause; a failure to look up display names leaves out only the display names, never rows; entries whose principal id starts with system: (Rancher's system principals, e.g. system://provisioning/...) carry system: true (accounts Rancher uses internally, not bindings an administrator added)), its machines (CAPI Machine objects in fleet-default filtered by the cluster.x-k8s.io/cluster-name label; each entry reports name, phase, and the first failing condition message - preferring conditions whose reason contains "Error"; a failed list leaves the machines field out of the JSON while the text output shows machines: unavailable, with a warning naming the cause; left out when the provisioning cluster was not found), and the commands in the default cluster registration token: nodeCommand and insecureNodeCommand (to add nodes), command and insecureCommand (to import a cluster), and manifestUrl. On an imported cluster (provisioning spec.rkeConfig absent), notApplicable lists the node command fields that are present but do not apply; such fields are marked, never left out. By default the registration section holds only a message and a hint, and the commands are left out, because they contain the cluster registration token (a credential that lets anyone add nodes to the cluster); pass --registration to fetch and show them. Each section can be missing without affecting the others: provisioningNote marks a confirmed missing provisioning Cluster; an unavailable or ambiguous lookup and a failed registration read leave out their sections with a warning naming the cause. If you cannot read part of the data, the command still exits 0: each section it could not read in full is named in data.degraded ({section, state, code, target}), and each entry has one warning. Finding the cluster by id or name and reading its management.cattle.io Cluster are required: the command fails when any of them fails. Sections that can degrade: provisioning (unavailable - the lookup of the provisioning.cattle.io Cluster that matches this cluster, one entry covering the status, machinePools, and machines, which are then left out), machines (unavailable - a machine list that failed after that Cluster was found), members (unavailable - the binding list; a failure to look up display names stays a warning), registration (unavailable - reading the cluster registration token).

Finding the user and reading it are required: the command fails when any of them fails; every other section can be unavailable. The argument accepts a user id, username, displayName, or a fully qualified user principal (local://<id>, <provider>_user://<id>) - a fully qualified principal is the one way to name a user unambiguously when ids and display names collide. data.user carries id, username, displayName, enabled, principals, created, and system, plus everything Rancher records per user in UserAttributes: groups (the group memberships as Rancher last refreshed them, which also happens at login; a flat array of {principal, displayName, provider}), lastLogin, lastRefresh and needsRefresh (when Rancher last refreshed the user's group memberships, and whether they need a refresh), disableAfter and deleteAfter (per-user values that override the disable-inactive-user-after and delete-inactive-user-after settings), and extra (extra information for audit logs, listed by provider, then key, with a list of values for each key; Rancher writes principalid and username today). These fields are read together: when reading the UserAttributes fails for any reason other than the object not existing (a user who has never logged in has none), all of them are left out of the output - never shown as an empty list - and the failure is recorded in data.degraded; on a successful read, an optional field that is left out was not set. data.roles.{global,clusters,projects} lists the role bindings that exist for the user or any of their group principals. They show which role bindings exist and do not say what the user can do; only the server can answer that, and this command does not ask it. Each row has the same fields as a member row in inspect cluster and inspect project (principal, displayName, role, binding (the name of the GlobalRoleBinding, ClusterRoleTemplateBinding or ProjectRoleTemplateBinding), and system); clusters and projects group the rows by cluster or project, with a displayName when it can be looked up for that entry. Roles can be bound to the user's groups; when reading the groups fails, all three role sections are left out too (they could not be complete) and are recorded in data.degraded with groups.

commands.desc: Prints a kubeconfig whose user entry runs the rancher exec-credential plugin. One context reaches the cluster through the Rancher proxy. When the cluster has the Authorized Cluster Endpoint enabled and the multi-cluster-management feature is on, the file also carries the direct contexts Rancher's own kubeconfig carries: <entry>-fqdn when the endpoint names an fqdn, else one <entry>-<node> per control-plane node, and the direct context is current. When those contexts cannot be derived (the endpoint's feature is off, the nodes cannot be read, no control-plane node has an address), the proxy-only file is printed and one notice on stderr says why. The user entry's env records this config directory, absolute, and RANCHER_CLI_CREDENTIAL_STORE (empty when the directory declares its store, else the value set now): the file works for this user on this machine only. Notices on stderr say so, and name the stored login kubectl's exec plugin will use when it is not this session's. The exec entry names that login's recorded owner with --user-id, and the plugin hands kubectl only that user's tokens; a notice says when the login records no owner. When the login also recorded the auth config its tokens are made through, the entry names it with --auth-provider beside --user-id, and the plugin hands kubectl only tokens made through it; a login that recorded none gets no --auth-provider, and no notice. installHint says how to install rancher, or how to regenerate the file for another --exec-command.

Creates nothing; with no config directory there is nothing to delete.

commands.desc: Lists the recorded events, oldest first. The table shows the hour (UTC; each event stores only the hour), event name, command, outcome and exit code; -o json and -o yaml carry every stored field of each event. Events that cannot be read are skipped. In a development build with the telemetryupload experiment, a sent event is listed until the file that holds it is deleted. Creates nothing and works while recording is off.
commands.name: telemetry show

commands.desc: Shows whether recording is on, what decided it (the RANCHER_CLI_TELEMETRY variable, the telemetry key of config.yaml, or the default), the number of recorded events, the number of dropped events, the contract version (the version of the event format) and the config directory id (a random id stored for this config directory). It also says whether this build sends the events that later recorded runs store in this config directory (sendsEvents in -o json): a release build sends none, and a development build sends only with an upload endpoint and recording on; with no endpoint, the text has a sending: none line that gives the reason. In a development build with RANCHER_CLI_EXPERIMENT set, it also lists the active experiments and the upload endpoint. A development build with the telemetryupload experiment sends the stored events of finished hours to that endpoint at most once an hour, after a recorded run, never from the kubectl exec plugin; with an endpoint, status shows the last upload attempt, the next attempt, the events waiting, the events of the current hour, and a warning for an upload lock that cannot be read. Creates nothing and works while recording is off.
commands.name: telemetry status
commands.usage: Show whether usage recording is on and what is recorded, and any active experiments

commands.desc: Development builds with the telemetryupload experiment only. Sends the stored events of finished hours and of the current hour to the experiment endpoint now, without waiting for the hourly limit or a Retry-After wait, with the same upload lock, request limits and decisions as the automatic upload. Records its attempt: the next automatic attempt comes about an hour later. Takes at most 30 seconds. Never runs from the kubectl exec plugin, and a release build refuses it. Its own run records no event. Exits 0 whatever the endpoint answered. sent counts every event in a request the endpoint answered with a 2xx, including the ones it refused; refused says how many. The data holds sent, refused, dropped, httpStatus, noAnswer, nextAttempt, timeLimitReached and skipped. With --debug it prints one line before and one after each request on standard error.
commands.name: telemetry upload
commands.usage: Send the stored usage events now (development builds with the telemetryupload experiment)

commands.desc: Groups results by --by (namespace|project|node|pod). --namespace, --project, and --node are filters that narrow every grouping: --node keeps only pods scheduled on that node; --namespace with --project requires one of the project's namespaces. --by node accepts only --node; combining --by node with --namespace or --project is a validation error. --project without --by returns one row for each of the project's namespaces (namespace grouping filtered to the project). --by project --project X returns a single row for that project. If no pods match --namespace or --node, the command reads the namespace or node you named: a missing one is NOT_FOUND, and one you are not allowed to read adds a warning to the result (with --project, a namespace outside the project is a validation error; --by node --node reads the node first, and an unreadable node there is an error; --by project reads the namespace list, and an unreadable list is an error). If you cannot read part of the data, the command still exits 0: each section it could not read in full is named in data.degraded ({section, state, code, target}), and each entry has one warning. The command fails when any of these required reads fails: finding the cluster by id or name and listing the pods always; finding the project by id or name and listing the project's namespaces with --project; listing the namespaces with --by project, and listing the projects with --by project and no --project; listing the nodes with --by node, or reading the named node with --by node --node N. Section that can degrade: metrics (unavailable - the CPU and memory usage figures are left out; the request and limit totals are still shown). With --project, if the project has no namespaces, the command reads no pods or metrics: the result has no rows (with --by project --project X, a single row with zero requests and limits).

the mutation was not applied because a required gate flag (--apply, --yes, --allow-deprecated) was missing; the message names the flags
--dry-run was given to a command that does not mutate
more than one value matched and none was selected; the error lists the candidates the command holds

a write collided with existing state: a resource changed on the server since it was read, a name already exists, a server entry is registered with a different URL or CA, the config directory changed while the command ran, or the server answered 409
a config-directory lock was not released within the wait, usually because another rancher process is writing

authentication failed: the server rejected the credential (HTTP 401), Rancher refused the sign-in, the exchange with the identity provider failed or timed out, an environment URL was set without RANCHER_CLI_TOKEN, or the credential belongs to another Rancher user than the call names
the stored credential for the server entry was replaced by another config directory that shares this one's identity, or by a login in progress
a login for the server entry is in progress, or ended before it recorded its credential identity

a change of this directory's credential store has work left: the old copy of the credential it changed, or the store pin, is not settled yet; a second store change is refused until it is, and other commands proceed

the credential store this directory uses cannot be read or written right now: a locked keychain, a keychain prompt that was cancelled, a keychain that cannot be reached, or a credential helper that is missing, timed out or failed; the message names the store, the entry, the cause as far as it is known, and the remedy

no such resource, server entry, or name: the server answered 404 for an object or for an API through a downstream cluster, the config directory has no such entry, or the name matched nothing in already-fetched data; when the command holds the list of names it could have meant, the error lists them as candidates
the server denied the request for lack of permission (HTTP 403)
the request was refused before or by the server: a missing or invalid flag or argument, a mutation under read-only mode, a disabled feature, or an object the server refused (HTTP 400 or 422)
the command requires Rancher Prime and the connected server does not have it
the server's TLS certificate is not trusted and was not accepted
the workflow the command needs is not supported by the connected server or by this CLI
the command was ended by Ctrl-C or a termination signal
an error with no more specific code, including a server or transport failure
